passage:
I'm Alka, Darshan's classmate. Right before the inter-school quiz final, I found him outside the hall, holding his stomach.
"I think I'm sick," he said. "My stomach's churning. I should tell Sir I can't do it."
I asked him when he'd last eaten. He looked surprised. He'd skipped lunch to revise. Then he said his hands were sweaty and his heart was going fast, but in a good way, sort of, like before a cricket match.
He stood there a minute with his eyes closed. I don't know exactly what he worked out. But he opened them and said, "I'm hungry. And nervous. And a bit excited." He ate the banana from my bag.
Twenty minutes later he answered the first question in the buzzer round.

qa.q: What had Darshan skipped to revise?
qa.a: He had skipped lunch to revise.

qa.q: What might Darshan have been feeling outside the hall?
qa.a: He may have been a mix of hungry, nervous and excited, though at first he thought he was sick, and Alka can't be sure of everything he felt.

qa.q: What helped Darshan read his body correctly?
qa.a: Slowing down to notice the whole pattern: when he last ate, his sweaty hands and fast heart, instead of guessing from the churning stomach alone.

qa.q: How might Alka have seen Darshan's worry outside the hall?
qa.a: Alka seemed to suspect it wasn't illness, which is why Alka asked when he had last eaten and shared the banana.

grounding: It shows a teenager unsure whether a churning stomach means illness, hunger, nerves or excitement, and working it out by slowing down to notice the whole pattern.

passage:
Monday. Before dance rehearsal, Kashish's stomach churned. She decided she was hungry and ate two plates of poha. The churning got worse, and now she felt heavy too. She messed up the second sequence and went home sure she'd eaten something bad.
Wednesday. Her friend Gopika, who'd danced for years, listened and asked, "When your stomach churns, are your hands cold? Is your heart fast?"
"Yes, both."
"That sounds more like nerves than hunger. Hunger for me is hollow and grumpy, and it comes when I haven't eaten for ages."
Kashish tried noticing more than just her stomach at practice that evening.
Saturday, the show. Backstage, the churning came again. Kashish stopped and checked: fast heart, warm face, a fizzy wanting-to-go-on feeling. Not hunger. Not only fear. Excitement. She breathed out slowly, grinned, and walked into the lights.

qa.q: What did Kashish eat before Monday's rehearsal?
qa.a: She ate two plates of poha.

qa.q: What did Kashish realise she was feeling backstage on Saturday?
qa.a: She realised the churning, fast heart and warm face meant excitement, not hunger and not only fear.

qa.q: What approach helped Kashish, and why did it work?
qa.a: Noticing the whole pattern, not just her stomach, so she could tell nerves, hunger and excitement apart.

qa.q: How does Gopika see Kashish's Monday mistake?
qa.a: Gopika sees it as a common mix-up and gently helps by describing how hunger and nerves feel different for Gopika.

grounding: It shows a teenager mistaking a nervous stomach for hunger, then learning to notice the whole body pattern and recognise excitement.

passage:
Ganga: I think I'm going to throw up. my stomach is doing somersaults
Pooja: the play's in an hour! are you sick??
Ganga: maybe? or maybe I'm dreading it. I think I should tell Ma'am I can't do it
Pooja: wait. slow down. when did you last eat?
Ganga: …breakfast? I skipped lunch for rehearsal
Pooja: ok. and how's the rest of you? hands, face, heart?
Ganga: heart fast. but I keep smiling for no reason. and I actually can't wait to wear the costume
Pooja: that sounds like hungry + excited, not dreading
Ganga: oh
Pooja: eat the banana in your bag. then see
Ganga: ok it's gone. stomach calmer. still fluttery but a good fluttery 🙂
Pooja: told you. break a leg

qa.q: What did Ganga skip for rehearsal?
qa.a: Lunch.

qa.q: What did Ganga first think the churning stomach meant?
qa.a: Ganga thought it meant being sick or dreading the play, and felt anxious enough to want to quit.

qa.q: What helped Ganga read the body signals correctly?
qa.a: Slowing down to notice the whole pattern: no lunch, a fast heart, smiling and looking forward to the costume.

qa.q: How might Pooja have felt when Ganga talked of quitting?
qa.a: Pooja was probably worried at first, then glad to have asked questions instead of agreeing.

grounding: Shows a teenager misreading a churning stomach as dread, then noticing the whole pattern and recognising hunger and excitement.

passage: The kabaddi selection was at the district ground in Karnal, and Simran, fifteen, stood by the bus stand with her stomach churning. 'I can't do this,' she told her teammate Zubin. 'I feel sick. I'm too scared. Let's just go home.' Zubin frowned. 'You've been talking about this selection for a month.' Simran sat on the low wall. Her Nani's words came back: stop, and notice all of it. So she did. Stomach churning. Hands tingling, but not cold. A grin she couldn't stop when she thought of the ground. And a hollow feeling: she'd been too nervous to eat breakfast. 'I think,' she said slowly, 'I'm hungry and excited. Not only scared.' She ate the roti in her bag. The churning eased. When the bus came, she got on.

qa.q: Where was the kabaddi selection?
qa.a: At the district ground in Karnal.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling by the bus stand at first?
qa.a: She felt sick and scared, wanting to go home.

qa.q: What helped Simran understand her body better?
qa.a: Stopping to notice the whole pattern, which showed hunger and excitement as well as nerves.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt when Simran wanted to go home?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and puzzled, since she had talked about the selection for a month.

grounding: Shows a teenager misreading a churning stomach as pure fear, and slowing down to notice the whole pattern of hunger and excitement.

passage: At Warsaw airport, Olga, sixteen, waited for Fatima, her pen-pal from Morocco, whom she'd written to for two years but never met. Her stomach was churning so hard she thought she might be ill. What if Fatima didn't like her? What if this was a terrible idea? She almost texted her mother to take her home. Then she made herself stop by the window and check. Heart fast. Cheeks warm. A silly smile each time the arrival board changed. And she'd had nothing but a coffee since morning. This wasn't dread. It was excitement, and hunger, all mixed up. She bought a pastry and ate it slowly. When Fatima came through the gate, waving wildly, Olga's stomach flipped again, and this time she knew exactly what it meant. She ran to hug her.

qa.q: How long had Olga written to Fatima?
qa.a: For two years.

qa.q: What did Olga first feel while waiting at the airport?
qa.a: She felt anxious and churned up, afraid Fatima might not like her.

qa.q: How did Olga figure out what her body was saying?
qa.a: She stopped to notice her fast heart, warm cheeks, silly smile and empty stomach, and recognised excitement and hunger.

qa.q: How might Fatima have felt coming through the gate?
qa.a: Fatima was probably excited and a little nervous too, waving wildly.

grounding: Shows a teenager misreading a churning stomach as dread and slowing down to notice the whole pattern of excitement and hunger.

passage: In the green room behind the school auditorium, ten minutes before the inter-school debate, Tushar's stomach churned like a washing machine. "I'm going to be sick. I can't go on," he told Ms Seema, the debate coach. She didn't argue. "Let's slow down. When did you last eat?" He thought. He'd skipped lunch to practise. "And what else is your body doing?" "Hands cold. Heart fast. But... I also keep grinning." "So some of it might be hunger, and some might be excitement, not only fear." She handed him a banana from her bag. He ate it, breathed out slowly twice, and noticed the churn had shrunk to a flutter. When his name was called, the flutter felt almost like a drumroll.

qa.q: Why had Tushar skipped lunch?
qa.a: He had skipped lunch to practise.

qa.q: What did Tushar first think his churning stomach meant, and what else was going on?
qa.a: He thought he was too scared to go on, but he was also hungry and a bit excited.

qa.q: How did Ms Seema help Tushar read his body better?
qa.a: She slowed him down, asked about food and other signals, and helped him see the whole pattern before deciding it was fear.

qa.q: What would have changed if Ms Seema had simply told Tushar not to be nervous?
qa.a: He might have stayed hungry and convinced he was only afraid, and perhaps pulled out of the debate.

grounding: Shows a teenager misreading a churning stomach as pure fear, and slowing down to notice the whole pattern of hunger, nerves and excitement.
